strengths: The paper proposes GROD, a pipeline that combines synthetic OOD generation (PCA/LDA boundary expansion), Mahalanobis-distance filtering, a binary ID-OOD loss, and post-processing for transformer-based OOD detection. The idea is practical and relatively efficient, with no extra parameters at inference time.

It attempts to provide a PAC-style theoretical treatment for OOD detection in transformer hypothesis spaces, extending prior OOD-detection learnability work with transformer approximation results. This is a potentially interesting direction.

The empirical study covers both CV and NLP tasks, multiple ID/OOD dataset pairs, several baselines, ablations on key hyperparameters/modules, and feature/likelihood visualizations. The experimental breadth is a clear effort.
The implementation and training details are mostly provided in appendices, and the method is described step-by-step, which supports some reproducibility.
The paper identifies an important practical problem: improving transformer generalization and ID/OOD boundary sharpening without OOD exposure during training.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claim is not supported. In Table 3 (CIFAR-100 ID, PCA-only), CIDER has better average FPR@95 (35.97 vs. 35.20), AUROC (91.57 vs. 91.34), and AUPR_OUT (92.06 vs. 91.49) than GROD. Table 4 likewise shows CIDER better average FPR@95. Yet the abstract and conclusion claim SOTA regardless of data format.

The near-perfect results in Table 2 (0.12% average FPR@95, 99.98% AUROC, 99.97% AUPR) are implausible for standard OOD benchmarks and are not sufficiently explained. The jump in Table 6 from average F=10.36/A=97.89 to F=0.12/A=99.98 when only adding Mahalanobis filtering is unexplained and suggests an evaluation or training artifact rather than a robust methodological improvement.

The theoretical results are not convincingly connected to the proposed algorithm. The key condition l(y2,y1) ≤ l(K+1,y1) from Theorems 4/5 is not enforced by the combined cross-entropy and binary ID-OOD loss in Eq. 11–13. The paper informally argues that L2 penalizes OOD misclassification, but this is not a rigorous derivation of GROD from the PAC conditions.

Theorem 5's lower bound contains unspecified constants and an exponent (K+1)^{n+1}, which for realistic n and K is generally vacuous. The theory therefore does not provide meaningful practical guarantees for the claimed algorithm.

Much of the theoretical contribution appears to extend Fang et al. (2022) by substituting transformer approximation results. The novelty is limited, and the “if and only if |X| < ∞” learnability condition is inherited from prior work rather than newly established for transformers.

The method's generality is questionable. LDA-based inter-class OOD generation is used for CIFAR-10 and text tasks but apparently avoided for CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-200; the paper states this is for stability, which contradicts the claim of broad applicability across data types.

The evaluation protocol around test-time LOGITS adjustment (Eq. 14) and the VIM post-processor is ad hoc and potentially test-time label-leaking: samples predicted as class K+1 are assigned uniform logits before post-processing. This could artificially inflate OOD detection metrics and is not ablated independently.

Synthetic OOD generation depends heavily on the current feature space, PCA/LDA projections, and Mahalanobis heuristic thresholds. There is no “gold standard” for virtual OOD quality, and the paper does not sufficiently analyze failure cases where generated OOD is ID-like or where the current feature space is unreliable.

Presentation quality is poor in several places: broken references (some entries replaced by placeholder text), duplicated words (“where where”), mislabeled tables (“Table 4.2”), inconsistent notation (e.g., H_mod vs. H_tood), and garbled equations. These issues impede verification and reproducibility.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section. The conclusion mentions future work and trade-offs, but it overclaims “rigorous mathematical foundations” and “SOTA” despite mixed results and unresolved empirical anomalies.

Baseline comparisons for text classification exclude ODIN and G-ODIN due to format incompatibility, which is reasonable, but the remaining baselines and the modified inference procedure make it difficult to assess whether gains come from GROD or from the post-processing/label adjustment scheme.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant problem: improving transformer generalization and OOD detection under distribution shift, with potential relevance to safe deployment.

The proposed GROD pipeline is relatively lightweight in inference: it fine-tunes an existing transformer with synthetic feature-space outliers and reuses a standard post-processor (VIM) without adding inference-time parameters.
The empirical study covers both image and text OOD detection benchmarks and includes ablations over key hyperparameters (gamma, alpha, num) and modules, as well as t-SNE/likelihood visualizations.
The paper attempts to connect algorithmic design to PAC/strong learnability theory for OOD detection, adapting prior FCNN-based results to a transformer hypothesis space.
Some reported results, especially Table 2 with CIFAR-10 as ID and LDA-generated OOD, are very strong and suggest the core idea could be promising if validated under a cleaner protocol.
weaknesses: Soundness and evidence: The headline empirical results are implausibly strong. GROD reaches FPR@95 around 0.1% and AUROC around 99.98% for near-OOD settings such as CIFAR-10 vs CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10 vs Tiny ImageNet, which is far outside typical OOD benchmark ranges and raises serious concerns about evaluation leakage, unfair tuning, or an implementation artifact. The paper provides no robustness checks, confidence intervals, or analysis to explain the near-perfect performance.

Overclaiming: The abstract claims SOTA 'regardless of data format', but Table 3 and Table 4 do not support this. For example, in Table 3 GROD's average AUROC is below CIDER (91.34 vs 91.57), and in Table 4 GROD's average FPR@95 is worse than CIDER (18.26 vs 15.97). These contradictions are not reconciled.

Theory is not presented soundly. The formal Theorem 5 uses an exponent 'm_h^{2n-1}' even though n is the data size, while the underlying approximation estimate in Lemma 3 uses 'm_h^{2 alpha -1}'. This is not a minor typo: it makes the stated bound nonsensical. The paper also mixes 'necessary and sufficient' claims with previous impossibility/learnability results, and the transformer extension largely follows from known approximation theory rather than establishing a new PAC theory of OOD detection for transformers.

The proof appendix contains questionable steps and algebra. For example, the derivation around Lemma 5 and Eq. 46 manipulates probability inequalities without clear justification, and several lemmas rely on strong assumptions or imprecise constructions. The claimed error bound is not validated empirically or connected quantitatively to GROD.

The theory does not justify the algorithm. The learnability conditions concern finite data, separation, and loss ordering, but GROD's synthetic OOD generation via PCA/LDA boundary extension, Gaussian sampling, and Mahalanobis filtering is heuristic. There is no guarantee that synthetic outliers approximate real OOD data, especially for near-OOD cases, and no theoretical link between the filtering threshold and the stated generalization bound.

The experiments do not isolate the source of gains. GROD combines a binary ID-OOD loss, synthetic OOD generation, Mahalanobis filtering, random filtering, and VIM post-processing. Table 6 shows that individual components often do not improve over the baseline, while the full combination suddenly yields near-perfect OOD detection. This pattern is suspicious and demands careful analysis, not just module ablation.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or inconsistent. It is unclear whether baselines receive equivalent fine-tuning, hyperparameter search, and post-processing. Table 5 is malformed: the VIM row reports an ID ACC of 64.00 in a text task where ID accuracy should ordinarily be unaffected by post-processing, and several entries for the semantic-shift setting are missing. Such inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported numbers.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The abstract says 'The code is available a' with no usable link. Important details are missing or vague, including how lambda is learned, how PCA/LDA dimensions are chosen in each setting, how random filtering seeds are handled, how baselines were tuned, and whether hyperparameters were selected using OOD test data. The appendix references are also corrupted, making it difficult to trace key theoretical sources.

Originality is limited. The method combines known ingredients: synthetic outlier exposure, PCA/LDA projections, Mahalanobis-distance filtering, an ID-OOD binary loss, and VIM. It does not compare against several recent OOD synthesis methods that would be natural baselines, and the PCA/LDA boundary construction is not theoretically shown to be superior to simpler alternatives.

Presentation quality is poor. There are multiple malformed tables, missing values, inconsistent notation (e.g., separate space, density-based space, n vs alpha), typographical errors, broken references, and unclear equation numbering. This significantly impedes expert assessment and replication.

Limitations and broader impact are under-discussed. The paper mainly lists future work rather than analyzing failure modes, false-positive/false-negative trade-offs, near-OOD breakdowns, or safety-critical implications of deploying OOD detectors. An honest limitations section would not be penalized, but this paper does not sufficiently provide one.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: improving transformer generalization under out-of-distribution shifts while connecting OOD detection to PAC-style learnability.

The proposed GROD pipeline is relatively lightweight: it generates synthetic OOD embeddings in feature space, avoids exposing the model to real OOD data during fine-tuning, and integrates with standard post-processors such as VIM.
The empirical study spans both computer vision and NLP tasks, includes multiple ID/OOD dataset pairs, and supplements the main results with ablations, t-SNE visualizations, and likelihood analyses.
The appendices provide substantial detail, including pseudocode, implementation settings, and proof sketches, which makes the intended approach easier to inspect than many shorter submissions.
weaknesses: The evaluation appears to tune hyperparameters directly on the OOD test sets. Figure 3 selects gamma, alpha, and num using OOD metrics on CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet, and SVHN; the main image results in Tables 2-4 then report on the same OOD datasets. This test-set leakage makes the SOTA claims unreliable and is a decisive methodological flaw.

The reported image results are implausibly strong. Table 2 gives average FPR@95 = 0.12% and AUROC = 99.98%, and the ablation in Table 6 shows that adding Mahalanobis filtering alone jumps from roughly FPR@95 = 10.36% / AUROC = 97.89% to FPR@95 = 0.12% / AUROC = 99.98%. Such near-perfect OOD detection on CIFAR-10 versus CIFAR-100/Tiny ImageNet with ViT-B-16 is far outside typical OpenOOD benchmark behavior and is not supported by error bars, repeated runs, or independent validation.

The theory-practice link is not established. Theorems 4 and 5 rely on conditions and universal-approximation results from prior work; the paper does not prove that the proposed binary loss L2 and the generated fake OOD data satisfy the required misclassification-penalty condition or approximate real OOD sufficiently. Thus the claim that GROD 'guarantees learnability' is substantially overstated.

The synthetic OOD generation is under-specified. The paper repeatedly refers to PCA^{-1} and LDA^{-1} as inverse mappings 'according to set theory', but PCA and LDA are dimensionality-reducing projections that are generally not invertible. Mapping selected boundary points from the reduced space back to the original feature space is therefore ambiguous and not reproducible as written.

Reproducibility is further weakened by unclear code availability (the link is truncated), missing main-experiment random seeds, and potentially unfair baseline tuning. For example, G-ODIN performs far worse than expected on image tasks, and ODIN/G-ODIN are excluded from text tasks, making the comparisons difficult to trust.

The presentation has multiple issues that hinder assessment: malformed tables, inconsistent theorem numbering between the main text and appendix, grammatical errors such as 'where where', and no explicit limitations or broader-impact discussion. These are not merely cosmetic because they obscure the exact protocol and claims.

strengths: Extends the PAC-style OOD detection learnability framework of Fang et al. (2022) to transformer hypothesis spaces, combining existing universal approximation and Jackson-type approximation results to derive capacity/depth-dependent learnability conditions and bounds.

Provides a theoretically motivated algorithm, GROD, that incorporates an ID-OOD binary classification loss and synthetic outlier generation; the method is architecture-agnostic and empirically evaluated across CV and NLP backbones.

Reports extensive experiments on image and text OOD detection, including ablations, computational cost comparisons, and t-SNE/likelihood visualizations, with generally strong empirical improvements over several baselines.
Partially acknowledges key limitations, such as the non-overlap assumption, loose/sufficient approximation bounds, and the gap between theoretical existence and trainability.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely incremental: the main learnability condition reduces to |X| < infinity plus sufficient transformer capacity, relying heavily on already-known FCNN/VC-dimension results and prior transformer approximation theorems. The transformer-specific part is mainly showing FCNN hypothesis spaces embed into transformers, not a fundamentally new OOD learning theory.

The central mathematical presentation is problematic. Definition 4.4 defines a “probability of OOD detection learnability” using Lebesgue measure over distributions and an ill-defined limsup, which is not rigorously justified. Main-text Theorems 4.5 and 4.6 also contain malformed expressions and apparent typos (e.g., an exponent 2n−1 where 2α−1 seems intended, misplaced parentheses), making the claimed bounds hard to verify.

There is a significant theory–algorithm gap. The theory only motivates auxiliary outliers and a penalty on OOD misclassification, but GROD’s PCA/LDA/Mahalanobis/soft-label/random-filtering pipeline is heuristic and not derived from the theory. The paper does not prove that the practical loss satisfies the required condition l(y2,y1) ≤ l(K+1,y1), nor does it provide guarantees when the non-overlap assumption is violated.

The empirical claims of “state-of-the-art” and “consistently” are overstated. For example, on ImageNet-200 the FPR@95 is worse than CIDER, and in NLP tasks some AUPR_OUT results are not best. Main tables lack error bars despite the claimed five random seeds, and the very large gains may partly reflect benchmark-specific synthetic OOD tuning.

Related-work positioning is inconsistent: the introduction suggests OOD detection is learnable in the separate space iff |X| < infinity, while Section 4.1 states it is not learnable unconditionally in that space, which confuses the theoretical narrative.

Writing and reproducibility need substantial improvement: the code URL is missing in the manuscript, notation is inconsistent (e.g., R vs. mathbb{R}, alpha/beta symbols), and there are numerous typos and awkward phrasings (e.g., “Abaltion”, “a-priori-unknown”).

The paper does not empirically validate the theoretical bounds or scaling laws; the Gaussian-mixture experiments illustrate the theory–training gap but do not directly verify Theorems 4.3, 4.5, or 4.6. Ethical discussion is also generic and does not address potential harms of OOD detection deployment.

strengths: Targets a genuinely important and under-theorized problem: transferring OOD-detection PAC learnability to transformer hypothesis spaces, which the paper correctly notes has been neglected relative to FCNN-based analyses (Fang et al., 2022).

The theoretical program is coherently organized: Lemma 4.1 (FCNN-based space is a subset of the transformer space) and Lemma 4.2 (transformer UAP tailored to OOD classification) are reasonable building blocks for importing existing learnability results, and constructive capacity conditions (depth/width) are offered in Theorem 4.3.

The proposed GROD algorithm is simple, architecture-agnostic, and only requires features plus logits, which in principle makes it compatible with many backbones; the paper evaluates it on both vision (ViT-B-16) and NLP (BERT, GPT-2, Llama-3.1-8B) backbones and several OOD shift types.

The empirical section is broad in scope, comparing against a sizable set of OpenOOD baselines and including computational-cost and ablation analyses, and the reported numbers, if corroborated, would be notable.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty. The central learnability theorem (Thm 4.3) yields the same necessary-and-sufficient condition as Fang et al. (2022), namely |X| < +∞; the advance over prior work is essentially swapping the FCNN UAP lemma for a transformer UAP lemma. The abstract's claim of establishing conditions 'for data distribution and model configurations' overstates the delta.

The learnability-probability bounds (Thms 4.5/4.6) appear vacuous for realistic settings: the bound is P ≥ (1 − O(1/m_h^{2α−1} + (m_h/r)^β))^{(K+1)^{n+1}}. With exponent (K+1)^{n+1} growing combinatorially in the number of datapoints n and classes K, the right-hand side is essentially 0 (i.e., trivially ≤ 1) unless the approximation error is exponentially small in n. The derived 'scaling law' claim (Remark C.11) therefore does not follow convincingly, and the Taylor expansion there even mis-writes the exponent as (K+1)^{α+1} instead of (K+1)^{n+1}.

Weak and loose coupling between theory and algorithm. The theorems assume non-overlapping ID/OOD distributions and no access to real OOD data, but GROD's specific design (PCA/LDA boundary extension, Mahalanobis filtering, soft-label construction, autoregressive centers) is entirely heuristic and is not derived from or shown to satisfy the theorem's sufficient conditions. The paper asserts the algorithm 'aligns more closely' with the learnable conditions without a rigorous argument.

Empirical results are implausibly strong and inadequately justified. Table 1 reports average FPR@95 = 0.12% and AUROC ≈ 99.98% on CIFAR-10, with near-OOD (CIFAR-100) at FPR@95 = 0.16% — far beyond typical OpenOOD benchmark ranges and essentially perfect separation. No variance/confidence intervals are reported in the main tables, and no mechanism explains why synthetic-outlier fine-tuning would beat methods that use real auxiliary OOD data (OE, MIXOE) by such large margins. This raises unresolved concerns about evaluation protocol, potential feature leakage from ID-derived synthetic outliers, or an unfair-advantage/benchmark-mismatch issue.

The claim of 'consistently SOTA performance across various data formats' is not supported by the NLP results. On Llama-3.1-8B background shift (Table 3) the method obtains AUROC ≈ 67% with FPR@95 ≈ 83%, and GPT-2 results are mixed; these are not state-of-the-art and partially contradict the abstract and conclusion.

Reproducibility gaps. The code link is missing/blank ('The code is publicly available at' with no URL), and much of the algorithmic and proof detail is deferred to appendices whose internal consistency is hard to verify (e.g., inconsistent equation/section references, variables such as 'm_FF', 'w', and 'num' used before definition).

Presentation quality is poor and undermines verification: numerous typos and notational inconsistencies (e.g., Y vs V, D_{X_I V_I}^α vs D^n in Def 1.1, subscript l vs I in Def 4.4), garbled and mis-dated references (e.g., Hendrycks & Gimpel 2016 cited as 2022; Fang et al. listed with inconsistent years), and heavy notation introduced without adequate clarity.

Limitations are not honestly surfaced for the central claims. Appendix C.12 concedes the bound is not tight, and Appendix H concedes applicability limits, but the main text does not acknowledge that the probability bound is practically vacuous or that the theory-to-algorithm link is heuristic; the impact statement is also perfunctory.

strengths: Extends PAC/strong learnability theory for OOD detection to a transformer hypothesis space, leveraging existing transformer approximation results to give necessary/sufficient conditions, approximation rates, and capacity-dependent error bounds.

Provides a broad empirical evaluation of the proposed GROD algorithm across image and text tasks and multiple transformer backbones (ViT-B-16, BERT, GPT-2, Llama-3.1-8B), with ablations over key hyperparameters and modules.

The paper attempts to bridge theory and practice by using theoretical insights to motivate an ID-OOD auxiliary loss and synthetic outlier generation, and it includes qualitative visualizations of generated OOD features and prediction likelihoods.

The limitations and applicability discussion is honest in places, e.g., acknowledging that the transformer class studied does not cover all modern architectures and that the theory does not pin down exact convergence rates.
No obvious human-subject or research-ethics concerns; experiments use public benchmark datasets and standard evaluation metrics.
The theoretical framing could be useful for the OOD detection community, especially the connection between learnability probability, model width/depth, and data complexity.
weaknesses: The central algorithmic claim—that GROD is theoretically grounded—is not adequately supported. The PAC theory establishes existence/learnability for some transformer in the hypothesis class, but it does not formally justify the specific PCA/LDA boundary sampling, Mahalanobis filtering, soft-label construction, or binary auxiliary loss used by GROD.

The empirical results are implausibly strong: e.g., CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-100/Tiny ImageNet/SVHN reaches ~99.98% AUROC and 0.12% FPR@95, far exceeding standard OpenOOD benchmarks. No error bars, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or leakage analyses are provided in the main tables, making it difficult to rule out overfitting or evaluation-protocol artifacts.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript states that code is publicly available, but the link is blank in the submitted version. The method contains many heuristics and hyperparameters, and without code it is hard to reliably reproduce the main results or synthetic OOD generation pipeline.

The presentation is difficult to follow: notation is overloaded and inconsistent (e.g., $n$ as both data amount and finite set size, $D_{X_I V_I}^{\alpha}$ typo, conflicting layer/budget definitions across theorem statements and appendices), and several theorem/lemma statements are informal or dimensionally mismatched for sequence-to-sequence transformers.

The theoretical novelty is incremental: the main learnability result largely transfers Fang et al. (2022) via prior transformer approximation lemmas from Jiang & Li (2023). The necessity proof for the full union hypothesis space is not rigorous, particularly when depth and width are unbounded.

The algorithmic novelty is also limited: GROD combines existing ideas—virtual outlier synthesis, PCA/LDA boundary sampling, Mahalanobis filtering, soft labels, and auxiliary OOD loss—without clearly isolating what is essential. Ablations are useful but do not demonstrate a fundamental advance over related virtual-outlier methods.

The main experiments do not validate the theoretical bounds. The authors state that validating theory through numerical experiments is too challenging due to local optima, but the paper then proceeds to claim that the algorithm aligns with and validates the theory, leaving a gap between formal results and empirical claims.

Fairness of comparison is unclear in places. GROD requires no real OOD data but is compared against outlier-exposure methods that use auxiliary OOD datasets, and the paper does not fully analyze whether the near-perfect gains come from the synthetic outlier construction, the post-processor, the pretrained backbone, or evaluation choices.
